For MAP estimates, you would need to add the second derivative for the log of the Gaussian distribution w.r.t. θ (where the distribution contains μ, σ and θ, but for the default MAP setting μ=0 and σ = 1). It's not clear how this could be done for EAP scores though since they are integrated across a range of θ values, and therefore aren't really point estimates. Hope that helps.

Phil

These are residuals for each response pattern. However, when the data is sparse (i.e., response patterns are missing, or the expected value is well below 1 as in the standard chi^2 assumption) they are pretty unreliable.

>
> Suppose I also have itemfit output

> Data adjusted so that the lowest category score for every item is 0

> 1 Comfort 0.8609461  5.400696       6 0.4935

>
>
> Now my question is what extra information does "residuals" giving me about the items when I already have so many item-statistics telling me about goodness of that item?

Simple answer, not much, but really they are asking different questions. The S_X2 stat is about whether the 'item' fits a collapsed version of the data, and therefore is much more stable than the pattern level residuals since sparseness essentially disappears due to collapsing (and conditioning on the total score, see the references). The other result asks about pattern residuals, how well the model can predict the number of participants with a given response pattern.

Just to save another email, the answer to you other question is that the res from residuals() is a z value, so no df. This is because the (O - E)^2 / E is a chi^2 with df=1, and the signed square root of that is a z value.

Also, I looked into the ltm output from the margins() function. Apparently, it isn't consistent across analyses, so in order to directly compare it will depend on the estimation function used in ltm. For instance, here is with the graded and 2PL models run on separate data returning information about the two-way marginals (i.e., 2-way covariance relationships between all item combinations, as well as their respective residuals).

Phil

````
library(ltm)
library(mirt)

# graded response model
(mod <- mirt(Science, 1))
(lmod <- grm(Science))

# signed two-way marginal residuals (unsigned in ltm)
margins(lmod)
residuals(mod)

# dichotomous data
dat <- expand.table(LSAT7)

(mod <- mirt(dat, 1))
(lmod <- ltm(dat ~ z1))

# signed two-way marginal residuals....apparently some weird truncated output from ltm
residuals(mod)
margins(lmod)

#ltm seems to report only a fraction of the two-way tables. These two give the same numbers when matched
residuals(mod, tables = TRUE)
mm <- margins(lmod)
mm$margins
```

As well as a later one by the same authors in APM about more severe model violations. Cheers.

I encountered the following error when I was trying to do a DIF analysis on a bifactor model (set of 9 items, all items were administered on a 6 point-Likert scale, N=1858).

gender <- ordered(Data[,1])

ADMm <- '

Adm = 1-9'

Checking for DIF in 0 more items

Computing final DIF estimates...

Error in `*tmp*`[[i]] : subscript out of bounds

best,
Michael

No literature, just my idea of how analysts do DIF testing, either by adding/removing parameters one at a time or in sets, or sequentially testing for parameters and once DIF is found create a new base model to be used in the comparisons (the sequential approach).

It doesn't. Partially because multidimensional DIF is hard is should be done with caution.

> EM cycles terminated after 500 iterations.

> EM cycles terminated after 500 iterations

Yes, there is a generic ... argument which accepts parameters to be passed down the function call stack. So you can pass TOL = # if you'd like and the estimation functions will use it. Cheers.

#constrain first three slopes in general factor to be equal across groups
model <- mirt.model('G=1-9
                                CONSTRAINB = (1-3, a1)')
mod <- bfactor(data, specific, model2=model)
```

Good hunting.

Phil

messages.subject_clean: Degrees of freedom for S-X2 statistic
messages.body_plain:
Hi Irshad,

The S-X2 statistic is built conditional on the total score values, so if some total scores don't appear very often the tables with the expected values for each category will be sparse. Therefore, in order to fix this the categories are collapsed both across categories (for polytomous items only) and total scores. So, some items might have more sparseness than others, and therefore require more collapsing; thus, have lower degrees of freedom to work with.

That being said, if you are checking out the S-X2 to polytomous items I would recommend updating to the dev version. The CRAN version works fine, but it was a bit over zealous with collapsing across categories, where sometimes they collapsed to only a single expected value (which makes a chi^2 test useless for those particular scores). Doesn't seem to affect the statistic too much overall since the effect is pretty minor, but nonetheless a better implementation is available. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Priors, like constraints, can be specified by separating the syntax arguments with a comma. So this would do it:

model <- mirt.model('F = 1-5,
                                 PRIOR = (1-5, a1, lnorm, .2, .2), (1-5, d, norm, 0, 1), (1-5, g, norm, -1.386294, .2)

Note that the g parameter is a normal/Gaussian prior since internally they are transformed to logit values, log(g/(1-g)), for better numerical stability, so priors should also follow this form too. Here the mean value is determined by checking qlogis(.2) = -1.386294. Cheers.

Phil

Hello Phil,

For calibration purpose,  I observed that you need minimum 3 items to go to the calibration ( at least for Rasch model)

I was experimenting with the LSAT7 data, which has 5 items in it. I calibrated first 3 items separately using Rasch 1 factor model.

$GroupPars
    MEAN_1 COV_11
par      0  1.436

Then I calibrated all 5 items together.

> raschfit_full=mirt(data, 1, 'Rasch')
Iteration: 27, Log-Lik: -2664.901, Max-Change: 0.00010

> coef(raschfit_full)

    a1     d g u

par      0  1.022

If you see there is change in the values of the parameter d. I have not changed the response pattern (or number of examinees) for first three items in both calibration.

Now I have a little bit more questions this time. :)

1) Why there is a change in the values of the parameter?

2.A) Another question which I have is that suppose I already have calibrated item bank of K items. I get M (K>M) new uncalibrated items in future. Now what should be the good idea for calibrating these new items?

E.g. Suppose In a year I get some new items getting added to my item bank. So should I calibrate these M items at the end of the year when I have all the items.

My aim is to fetch the reliable estimates of item parameters.

3)  Last but not the least, Suppose I keep getting the more new responses to the already calibrated items ( through CAT (Computerized Adaptive Test)). These responses will be sparse as it is a CAT. The model is different. IRT is a multivariate technique, so when you add items in you change the definition of the θ parameters (generally measuring it better), as well as fit more coefficients with more degrees of freedom (here, 2^3=8 versus 2^5 = 32, total df, while fitting 4 versus 6 coefs).

>
> 2.A) Another question which I have is that suppose I already have calibrated item bank of K items. I get M (K>M) new uncalibrated items in future. Now what should be the good idea for calibrating these new items?

You could either refit everything, or treat the previous parameters as fixed/population values in the model and simply estimate the unknown coefs. Both approaches will work for estimating parameter variability by computing the standard errors.

>

It's generally a good idea to update your item parameters as time goes on for consistency. I'd recommend investigating what larger testing corporations like ETS do to keep their items valid and fresh.

Add in more response patterns to an IRT analysis will always improve the accuracy of the parameters (regardless of whether they are sparse or not), provided the new responses are from the same population. Stopping criteria is up to you: how precise do you need your estimates to be, and does it even matter if you have a relatively strict CAT stopping criteria? messages.body_plain:
Hi Ross,

You can generally modify the plot elements by passing named arguments to the function which are later caught by the lattice package. However, I don't think they're a default way to do the Edwards plot in the package (seems like a fairly customized plot). You'll have to build them up. Something like this should work:

```
library(mirt)
library(latticeExtra)

dat <- key2binary(SAT12,
                   key = c(1,4,5,2,3,1,2,1,3,1,2,4,2,1,5,3,4,4,1,4,3,3,4,1,3,5,1,3,1,5,4,5))
mod <- mirt(dat, 1)

Theta <- seq(-3,3, by=.01)
TI <- testinfo(mod, Theta)
TI2 <- TI - 1
plt <- data.frame(test=rep(c('test_1', 'test_2'), each=length(Theta)),
                  Theta=c(Theta, Theta), TI=c(TI, TI2),
                  SE=c(1/sqrt(TI), 1/sqrt(TI2)))

obj1 <- xyplot(TI~Theta, plt, groups = test, type='l', main = 'Title',
               xlab = expression(theta), ylab=expression(I(theta)),
               panel = function(x, y, groups, ...){
                   pick <- groups == 'test_1'
                   panel.xyplot(x[pick], y[pick], type = 'l', lty = 2)
                   panel.xyplot(x[!pick], y[!pick], type = 'l', lty = 1)
               })
obj2 <- xyplot(SE~Theta, plt, groups=test, type='l', ylab=expression(SE(theta)),
               panel = function(x, y, groups, ...){
                   pick <- groups == 'test_1'
                   panel.xyplot(x[pick], y[pick], type = 'l', lty = 2)
                   panel.xyplot(x[!pick], y[!pick], type = 'l', lty = 1)
               })
doubleYScale(obj1, obj2, add.ylab2 = TRUE)
```

Probably too verbose, but still it's possible. Another option is just to use base plots, which may or may not be easier. Cheers.

Phil

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been fitting bifactor GRMs and started noticing a strange behavior with the anova function. Upon closer look it appears that it gives negative X2 depending on the order the models are passed.

I should say I'm not a specialist in R or MIRT, but my best guest by looking at the sources is that, since the difference in the dfs is 0, it is not changing the order of object and object2 before evaluating the LRT. I am still a little fuzzy on why the dfs are the same for different bifactor models, but I think abs(2*object2@logLik - 2*object@logLik) would be a theoretically valid fix?

Minimal example:
T <- matrix(sample(1:5,1600, replace = T), ncol = 4)
x <- bfactor(T, c(1,1,2,2), itemtype = 'graded')
x2 <- bfactor(T, c(1,1,2,3), itemtype = 'graded')
# X2 > 0
anova(x2,x)
# X2 < 0 (I guess models aren't technically "nested" in this order)
anova(x,x2)

Thanks for any clarifications on this!
--Chamon

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luiz,

You are correct that anova doesn't sort these objects because df1 - df2 = 0, so the function doesn't really know which is nested in the other. In this example, there is no nesting since the same number of parameters are estimated in both models (neither are uniquely identified, but thanks for the small example).

I've generally avoided using abs() to fix the differences because when using the MHRM algorithm the log-likelihoods are approximated by Monte Carlo estimation, so models that are very close may actually have higher log-likelihoods in the nested model due to simulation inaccuracies. And I think it's good to be aware of that in day-to-day analyses.

Either way, when comparing models with the same number of parameters the best one can really do is use information statistics, so I wouldn't be so worried about the X2 difference. Cheers.

Phil
